name: Bitwarden
tagline: Open-source password manager with hosted and self-hosted options

pricing.notes: Official pricing checked 2026-07-30; Premium listed at $1.65/month billed annually ($19.80/year).
pricing.freeTier: Free covers unlimited passwords, devices and passkeys; Premium adds TOTP and reports.

tiers.name: Free (individual)
tiers.limits: 1 user; unlimited passwords, passkeys and devices; share with 1 other Bitwarden user; text-only Send.

tiers.name: Free organization
tiers.limits: 2 users and 2 collections; unlimited vault items.

tiers.name: Premium
tiers.limits: 1 user; unlimited passwords/devices; 5 GB personal attachment storage; up to 10 hardware security keys.

tiers.name: Families
tiers.limits: Up to 6 users; unlimited collections; 5 GB personal storage plus 5 GB organization storage.

tiers.name: Teams
tiers.limits: Unlimited users and collections; Premium features for every seat; 5 GB personal plus 5 GB organization storage.
tiers.notes: Published price is per user/month billed annually; 7-day business trial.

tiers.name: Enterprise
tiers.limits: Unlimited users and collections; includes SSO, account recovery, self-hosting and 1 Families sponsorship per user.
tiers.notes: Published price is per user/month billed annually; 7-day business trial.

pricing.freeTierCaps: Free individual: 1 user, unlimited passwords/passkeys/devices, sharing with 1 other user; Free organization: 2 users and 2 collections.
pricing.billingTerms: published prices are annual subscriptions; no public month-to-month prices displayed; taxes excluded
pricing.hiddenCosts: Extra encrypted storage costs $0.33/GB/month; organization seats added by invitations are prorated, and unused purchased seats remain billable until the subscription seat count is reduced.

verdictSummary: If your goal is to stop paying hosted Bitwarden Premium, the core vault can be self-hosted or replaced with KeePass-style local storage; the caveat is security responsibility.
coreLoopDIY: Use KeePassXC locally or self-host a Bitwarden-compatible server, keep encrypted backups, and use browser/mobile clients.
whyPeopleStillPay: They pay because a professionally maintained security service is cheap relative to the downside of mistakes.

priorArt.name: vaultwarden
priorArt.desc: Unofficial Bitwarden-compatible self-hosted server used by many technical users.

alternatives.name: AliasVault
alternatives.desc: Passwords, passkeys, and disposable inboxes in one vault; self-host it and mail delivery joins your chores.

facts.install: Hosted signup and browser/mobile apps, or a Linux Docker Compose install script for self-hosting
facts.dataFormat: Vault secrets and received-email contents are encrypted client-side; the hosted or self-hosted server stores ciphertext, with an offline cache on clients
facts.gapVsPaid: It does not yet match Bitwarden's mature Organizations, broad client ecosystem and recovery and sharing workflows.
facts.setupBlocker: None for the hosted service; self-hosting needs a Linux server, Docker, DNS/TLS and mail routing

alternatives.name: Bitwarden Free
alternatives.desc: The core password manager is already free: unlimited vault items, devices, passkeys, and autofill.

facts.install: Create a hosted account and install an official app or extension; optional self-hosting uses Bitwarden's Docker deployment
facts.dataFormat: Vault items are encrypted locally before sync; Bitwarden's cloud or a self-hosted server stores encrypted vault data, while clients keep an encrypted local cache
facts.gapVsPaid: It is the same core product, but canceling Premium means losing integrated TOTP, file attachments, emergency access and several reports.
facts.setupBlocker: None for hosted use; self-hosting requires Docker, a domain/TLS, SMTP and ongoing server maintenance

alternatives.name: KeePassXC
alternatives.desc: A vault file on your disk with excellent autofill; syncing and sharing are deliberately somebody else’s job.

facts.install: Native Windows, macOS and Linux package
facts.dataFormat: One encrypted KDBX database file on disk; syncing means placing that file in a separate cloud or shared-folder service
facts.gapVsPaid: It trades Bitwarden's built-in sync, sharing and account recovery for a single vault file that you must synchronize and back up safely yourself.
facts.setupBlocker: There is no built-in sync, sharing or recovery, so the user must choose a sync method and manage conflicts and backups

alternatives.name: Passbolt Community Edition
alternatives.desc: A team password vault with real sharing and a server stack that expects an adult in the room.

facts.install: Ubuntu or Debian package, or Docker deployment, followed by browser-extension setup
facts.dataFormat: Password secrets are OpenPGP-encrypted; account, sharing and audit metadata live in SQL, while users' private keys and recovery kits remain client-side
facts.gapVsPaid: It requires substantially more server and OpenPGP key administration while offering a narrower, team-first experience than Bitwarden.
facts.setupBlocker: A server, database, domain, TLS, SMTP and key-recovery process are required before anyone can use it

alternatives.name: Vaultwarden
alternatives.desc: Bitwarden’s clients pointed at your own server; unofficial, capable, and now you are the outage.

facts.install: Docker or Podman container with a persistent /data volume and a reverse proxy for HTTPS
facts.dataFormat: Client-encrypted Bitwarden-compatible vault data stored in SQLite by default, or MySQL/PostgreSQL, with attachments and configuration in the persistent volume
facts.gapVsPaid: It is unofficial and may lag Bitwarden's proprietary or enterprise features, while support, backups and uptime move to you.
facts.setupBlocker: Docker, a domain and HTTPS reverse proxy are the easy part; backups, upgrades and outages become the user's responsibility

rejectedAlternatives.name: Padloc
rejectedAlternatives.desc: The live site hides a stalled repo: last commit March 2025 and production self-hosting docs never really arrived.

notes: Interesting because the paid app itself has strong open-source/self-host lineage.
prompt:
Build me a self-hosted password vault to replace hosted Bitwarden Premium.
Requirements:

- Do not write a password manager. Deploy vaultwarden (the Bitwarden-compatible
  server) on my VPS: a docker-compose.yml with the vaultwarden/server image
  and a data volume at ./vw-data.
- Front it with Caddy for automatic HTTPS on a subdomain I give you; the
  browser and mobile clients require HTTPS to work at all.
- Lock it down after I register my one account: SIGNUPS_ALLOWED=false, admin
  token in .env, nothing else exposed.
- Clients are the official Bitwarden apps and extensions pointed at my server
  URL. That is the point: autofill, mobile, and passkeys keep working.
- Nightly backup cron job: tar vw-data, encrypt it with age, copy it off the
  box. Write restore.sh and make me run one restore drill before trusting it.
- Import my existing vault with the standard Bitwarden export/import flow.
- Out of scope: emergency access, org and family sharing, and pretending I
  have a security team. Note in the README: clients cache the vault, so a
  dead server locks me out of nothing, but I now own updates and patching
  forever.
- README: compose up, first-account creation, update procedure, and the
  restore drill.
